Job Kléber is 34 years old, he started to train muay thai and self defense after getting  inside the Police Department. He believes not everything is solved with a gun in your hands. And he proved that years later, when he was already on the squad of big events, and received the mission  of infiltrating himself on the manifestations that took over Brazil since June 2013. “I was called to work without my uniform among the protesters. My job was to stop the people who were armed and for that, we use the immobilization method of defense.”

The name might sound weird, but is in honor of his grandfather and that Job meand Jó, biblical figure in latim. Married with 2 kids, he needs to divide his time between the PD, personal security, training and family. “My wife complaints a lot, because is adrenaline all the time and I miss my family time. But I’m sure this will change,” he explains, that despite the difficulty, his family supports him with MMA.

Asked about his idols, he has a sharp answer – and is no Champion of the UFC. “My mom and dad, that worked hard to raise me. Actually my stepfather. We have hard times at home, but we never missed anything. “Today me and my Brothers work because they helped us.”  About his job, he talks about risking his life every day for people he doesn’t even know – and many times judge him wrong. “There are many good cops and no one stops to think how hard our work is.”

TRAINING: Early mornings start at 6am with coffee and my breakfast, then I head on down to the MMA Lab for one on one mitt work and then strength and conditioning. I go home and rest until team training at 3-5pm. I’m always working.

When and why did you start training for fighting? Fighting, in a way, fell into my lap. I have been an athlete my entire life, so competing in any sport came naturally for me. My twin sister, Jillian Lybarger, actually started training MMA before me. At her first fight, I witnessed her passion and drive for the sport and was inspired to do the same. The rest is history.

What ranks and titles have you held? RFA Strawweight World Champion
 
Do you have any heroes? I idolize Benson Henderson. I look up to him in every aspect of his life. I train next to him every day at The MMA Lab. He is always pushing me to get better. My hero is my wife, Jana. She is always taking care of me and our family when we need her. She loves me like no other. She makes me a better person. Win or lose, she will always love me.
 
What does it mean for you to fight in the UFC? Fighting in the UFC means the absolute world to me. It means that all the three a days, all the time away from my family, all the holiday meals I had to miss were not in vain. All the sacrifice has been worth it, all of my efforts validated. It means I can take care of my family like they deserve to be taken care of. I will now be able to do more for the organization (Cancer Treatment Centers of America) that I am so passionately involved in. It means the world title is there for me to take. This is a dream come true.
 
Did you go to college and if so where? San Diego Mesa
 
What was your job before you started fighting? A lead trainer for a boxing club
 
Specific accomplishments in amateur competition? Amateur Tuff –N-Uff 125 Champion
 
Ranks in any martial arts styles: Blue Belt in Jiu-Jitsu 
 
Favorite grappling technique: Triangle
 
Favorite Striking technique: Slip Jab

I own a yoga studio and when not in camp I teach yoga classes as well.

TRAINING: A typical day of training includes strength and conditioning in the mornings, 4 or 5 times a week. At night I work my grappling or striking, sometimes both. A few times a week, I try to get a workout in during the afternoon, in between. Every Saturday is sparring day. The whole team comes in and we finish the week by punching each other in the face. Then I have my cheat meal and rest on Sunday, to start all over again on Monday. I usually have my last cheat day and sparring day 2 weeks before the fight.

 When and why did you start training for fighting? I started training because I thought the guys in karate movies were cool.

What ranks and titles have you held? Black belt in BJJ, Freestyle Fighting Championship MW Champion (2004)

Do you have any heroes? My dad

What is your favorite technique? My favorite is whatever wins me the fight.  I seem to be very good at taking a fighter’s back and applying a RNC

What does it mean for you to fight in the UFC? To me, fighting in the UFC is a landmark in my career.

What was your job before you started fighting? Construction laborer.  I just worked to pay the bills so that I could train at night and fight on weekends.

Joseph Duffy’s UFC career hasn’t been a long one, but he’s proving very quickly that there’s more to like about Irish fighters than Conor McGregor.

In two lightweight bouts since joining the UFC in 2015, “Irish Joe” has two first-round finishes – a knockout of Jake Lindsey at UFC 185 in his debut and a triangle choke of Ivan Jorge at UFC Fight Night Glasgow.

Those wins improved Duffy’s MMA record to 14-1. But there’s more to consider: he has nine submission victories, four KOs and, incredibly, 12 first-round finishes.

He’s also the last man to beat McGregor, the current UFC interim featherweight champ, scoring a submission win in Nov. 2010.

Duffy, from Donegal, Ireland, began his professional career with 10 consecutive wins before sustaining his first loss, a fourth-round submission via guillotine choke to Ivan Musardo. He then inexplicably stopped competing in MMA.

“I think a lot of people were confused when I left the sport,” he told UFC.com. “Maybe some put it down to the loss. I just saw it as an opportunity to improve myself as a martial artist, and it’s an experience that I felt was very beneficial.”

Duffy turned to boxing, compiling a 7-0 record before injuries slowed his career and caused him to rethink his MMA career.

It was clearly a wise decision to come back. He returned to MMA in Aug. 2014, ending a 34-month hiatus, and scored first-round finishes over Damien Lapilus and Julien Boussuge. His continued upward trajectory since signing with the UFC has given Irish fans hope they might have another champion in the future

Duffy, 27, holds black belts in Japanese Jiu-Jitsu and taekwondo and a blue belt in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. His striking is a major weapon, but his submission work has been spectacular. Against Jorge at UFC Fight Night Glasgow, for example, Duffy reversed an apparent takedown and turned it into a triangle choke.

At the pace Duffy is going, there’s much more of that to come.

Ranks in any martial arts styles: Blue belt in BJJ under Scott Morton and Rodrigo Vaghi.
